doc.title: Johnny Varro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

chapter: Condon's circle and New York scene
title: Nick's versus Condon's informality
summary: Contrast of strict Nick's with Phil Napoleon and Pee Wee Irwin and the loose Condon's duo with Buzzy Drootin.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah. That whole scene, that as you said Condonites, what was it that made that almost a style in itself, the way those guys played or just their personalities?

Well the informality of it was very important. It was loose and relaxed. Well I’m going ahead of myself, but I’m going way ahead of myself, I don’t know how far do you want me to go on this thing. But I did work at Nick’s for a while, Nick’s with Phil Napoleon and later on with Pee Wee Irwin. And this is in the 50s, the mid-50s. And Nick’s was a very formal place. The music was very strict and they wanted you to play a certain style, two beat more or less, and don’t swing too much. Yeah, yeah really. I mean the bands were very precise and good, good groups, I mean a hell of a good bunch of bands, good players too. That’s when I first meet Kenny Davern, with Phil Napoleon — I’m sorry, with Pee Wee Irwin at Nick’s. And later on I worked, about two years later I got a call from Eddie Condon to work his saloon, as a soloist. Actually it was a duo with Buzzy Drootin on drums and myself. And I noticed the informality of that place, it was so much looser and easier going and they weren’t worried about whether you’re having a drink or stuff like that. You know, so some of us abused that privilege too.
